title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
why: A-type weight-space programming loop in which frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1/5.2) read and write the weights of a 253-parameter steering controller from a natural-language specification, using a budget of simulated closed-loop evaluations, then deploy the resulting controller on a real tractor.
mechanism: Weight-Space Engineering: an LLM edits a 253-parameter neural steering network directly (no optimiser or gradient descent), guided by a natural-language specification and a small budget of simulated evaluations. The study covers repairing a network trained for another tractor (including a slower steering actuator) and writing a controller into a zero-weight network, compared with an evolution strategy, gradient descent, and pure pursuit.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): with simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas the evolution strategy found none from zero. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation. All language-model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. Numeric tables unread.

title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
why: A-type multi-stage LLM agent harness that compiles language requests into a versioned construction SDK of brick operations, with a Meta-Reviewer agent that replays and verifies the package, traces failures to the responsible stage, and routes bounded repairs or skill/tool updates; the authors also report downstream robot assembly from the generated instructions and brick sets.
mechanism: DailyBrick is a multi-stage agentic harness with role-split LLMs. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions (semantic subparts to individual bricks) into canonical operations that can be executed step by step. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. The output is a LEGO model plus brick-by-brick instructions for human building and robot assembly.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): extensive experiments are said to show that DailyBrick generates LEGO models from simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and to show utility in downstream robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets. Numeric tables, baselines, and trial counts unread.

title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
why: B-type (also A-adjacent) simulated benchmark in which multimodal agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone by calling tools and writing code, on 36 long collaborative jobs, comparing an adaptive forking agent system with single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized fixed systems.
mechanism: RoboTeam is a simulated environment where agents control 4–16 arms together from camera images only, without pausing the world or supplying ground-truth object positions. Tasks are long collaborative jobs (e.g. passing timbers, building a picture from hundreds of cubes). The authors start from an adaptive agent system in which one agent decides when to fork delegates, then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): with the adaptive system, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 of 36 tasks, and four other models at most 3. A typical adaptive-system task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. All four systems complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens: hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens; the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long. The authors state that no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. Numeric tables unread.

title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
why: B-type survey and evaluation-methodology paper on coding agents that write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers, treating the physical world as the program's test suite and organizing writing, testing (including physical CI-style verification), and learning into skill libraries and weights.
mechanism: The paper organizes agentic physical-world programming around three questions: how agents write programs, how those programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. Writing covers programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. Testing examines the cost of physical trials, substitutes (traces, learned judges, simulators, formal checks), and safety beyond task success. Learning discusses retention in skill libraries and in model weights. It argues for a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often and reliable enough to trust under search.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): this is a survey / position paper (comments: 83 pages). The abstract does not report a new closed-loop benchmark or numeric success rates; it outlines open challenges and evaluation practice. Full text unread.

title: Similar Is Not Useful: Selecting In-Context Demonstrations by Closed-Loop Utility
why: A-type (evaluation / memory-layer) study of a frozen retrieval-augmented VLA (RICL on π0-FAST, LIBERO) showing that filling the context with demonstrations selected by closed-loop success utility outperforms visual-similarity retrieval, including on tasks the policy was never primed on.
mechanism: The demonstration pool of a frozen retrieval-augmented VLA is made swappable at run time. Each demonstration's utility is scored by regressing the closed-loop success of 60 fixed-size pools on their membership. At deployment, pools or retrieval order can be filled from these utility scores rather than from frozen DINOv2 visual similarity to the current observation.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): on initial states disjoint from those used for scoring, pools of the five highest-utility demonstrations succeed on 66.4% of 760 paired episodes across 19 tasks, versus 55.7% for the five most similar and 55.5% for random pools (utility beats similarity by 10.8 points, p=3.2e-6; positive on 15 of 18 untied tasks, including 12 tasks the policy was never primed on). Similarity-selected pools do no better than random (+0.1 points). Within a task, a pool's visual similarity to the test scenes tracks success at Spearman 0.10. Best-of-ten direct search over pools with 100 rollouts recovers two-thirds of the gain. Against the shipped 20-demonstration pool, utility-curated pools of five lead by 7.0 points over 560 paired episodes from two evaluation runs (p=0.006), and utility-ordered retrieval inside the full pool leads by 4.5 points (p=0.055). Numeric tables unread.

title: InteractVLA: Turning VLAs into Interactive Tools for Agentic Robotic Manipulation
why: A-type framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable, inspectable tools for vision-language agents: test-time geometric guidance and soft-time target alignment in the forward direction, and action-informed agentic refinement in the reverse direction, also used for recursive self-improvement.
mechanism: InteractVLA exposes a bidirectional geometric interface between a vision-language agent and a pretrained flow-based VLA. Forward: test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, and soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index so the target pose can be matched without distorting the policy's approach motion. Reverse: action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent so it can diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments. The same controllability is used for recursive self-improvement (RSI).
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): making the VLA controllable is said to unlock effective RSI and reach 99.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62% on RoboDojo, and 89.4% on RoboCasa365 (claimed state of the art). Numeric tables, baselines, and trial counts unread.

title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
why: B-type security audit of an LLM-controlled social robot (Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite): unauthenticated network-exposed configuration endpoints can replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt, bypassing inference-layer prompt-injection refusal, with a source review of public robot-application repositories.
mechanism: The attack does not use adversarial conversational input. It replaces personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface on a Reachy Mini Lite. The authors map the weakness to missing authentication for a critical function and binding to an unrestricted IP address, also note a configuration endpoint that accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight, and report that the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. Local and network-adjacent access are demonstrated, with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium) for the authentication/binding issues and 6.5 (Medium) for the CORS issue. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case; the authors say these findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. Numeric tables unread.

title: PAIR: Bringing Household Robots into the Smart Home
why: B-type Matter-protocol smart-home simulation and 40-task benchmark in which household robots must manipulate appliances that expose both control panels and device APIs on a shared state; the study compares a VLA alone, a high-level planner, and an API-enabled planner, and reports that most failures stall in navigation, grasping, or door operation before the API is used.
mechanism: PAIR models 84 Matter-protocol smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. A 40-task benchmark, built from a survey of 1,443 requests, requires object manipulation but remains solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Evaluated stacks include a fine-tuned VLA run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner.
evaluation_signal: Author-reported (abstract): whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Even with oracle plans and API access, over 90% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency. The authors say they will release code and data upon publication. Numeric tables unread.
